                                  PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                   §
                                                                       OF TEXAS
                                                  §
                                                  §

                SKYBOX DATACENTERS, LLC’S INITIAL COMMENTS

       Skybox Datacenters ("Skybox") appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on

proposed 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 25.194 to implement Public Utility Regulatory Act

(“PURA”) § 37.0561 regarding the implementation of interconnection standards for large loads in

the ERCOT region. As a leading developer of data center infrastructure in Texas, Skybox is

committed to the long-term reliability of the ERCOT grid. While Skybox supports the objective of

ensuring that large load interconnection requests are grounded in demonstrably viable and

committed projects, targeted refinements are necessary to avoid unintended impacts on advanced

stage projects and to ensure that financial requirements remain appropriately calibrated, non-

duplicative, and closely aligned with actual system risk and cost incurrence, without unfairly

penalizing currently mature projects or creating redundant financial barriers.

       Senate Bill 6 directs the Commission to establish standards that support business

development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.

Achieving these objectives requires a framework that: (i) aligns financial obligations with actual

cost incurrence and system risk; (ii) preserves regulatory certainty for projects that have already

advanced under existing processes; and (iii) avoids procedural or commercial requirements that

could delay interconnection studies and energization, while preventing distortions to efficient

project development.

       Data center developers and investors (interconnecting large load entities (“ILLEs”)—


                                                 1
 including Skybox), generation partners, and transmission and/or distribution service providers

(“TDSPs”) have invested substantial time and resources in ERCOT’s stakeholder process

addressing Batch Zero eligibility under Planning Guide Revision Request (“PGRR”) 145. Batch

Zero eligibility is intrinsically linked to the broader framework governing large load

interconnection standards, and therefore these efforts bear directly on, and are highly relevant to,

the issues presented in Project No. 58481. These activities have also been accompanied by

significant financial commitments—often in the millions or billions of dollars—made in reliance

on the regulatory framework in place at the time investment and development decisions were

undertaken. Skybox and other stakeholders recognize and support the need for a structured

approach—like batch/cluster studies--to managing the reliability and planning implications

associated with the rapid growth of large load interconnections, as reflected in continued and active

engagement in the ERCOT rulemaking and market development processes.

 I.      RECOGNITION AND TREATMENT OF ADVANCED STAGE (BATCH ZERO /
                         BASE LOAD) PROJECTS

       Project No. 58481 should expressly recognize that large load projects substantiated under

ERCOT’s prior “interim” interconnection process and current Planning Guide §§ 9.4 and 9.5

constitute advanced-stage load that has already satisfied the core readiness criteria underlying

newer screening constructs. Projects that have completed required studies, executed

interconnection agreements and demonstrated financial commitment through transmission and/or

distribution service provider (“TDSP”)-accepted mechanisms should be treated as fixed inputs for

planning purposes and should not be subject to re-screening, re-evaluation, or displacement based

on subsequently submitted requests.

       Any framework that conditions the continued advancement of such projects on re-

evaluation of previously completed studies or imposes new eligibility criteria based on


                                                 2
 retrospective cutoff dates alters the legal consequences of actions completed under the prior

framework and therefore operates retroactively, notwithstanding characterization as a prospective

process.

       This approach is consistent with SB 6 and PURA § 37.0561, which direct the Commission

to support business development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining

system reliability. Projects that have advanced under existing rules, secured site control, and

funded interconnection related infrastructure reflect reliance on the regulatory framework in place

at the time of investment and should not be subject to requalification under newly adopted

standards. These projects have already been evaluated and approved through ERCOT’s established

interconnection framework and represent mature developments that have demonstrated viability

through executed interconnection agreements, substantial financial commitments, and compliance

with applicable ERCOT and TDSP requirements. Imposing additional, retroactive financial

obligations on such projects would not yield incremental reliability benefits and would instead

create unforeseen capital burdens on infrastructure that is already well advanced in the

development cycle, contrary to cost causation principles and the objectives of SB 6.

       Accordingly, new or incremental financial requirements—such as a potential $50,000/MW

interconnection fee—should not apply to projects that have already demonstrated readiness

through an executed interconnection agreement, site control (lease or ownership), posted financial

security, and funded CIAC payments aligned with TDSP-determined interconnection costs.

Imposing additional requirements on these projects would not advance reliability objectives and

would introduce duplicative cost burdens inconsistent with cost causation principles. Projects that

qualify for, or should be properly categorized, as proposed Batch Zero “base load” in ERCOT’s

pending PGRR 145 are already experiencing approval delays that create unforeseen financial and



                                                3
 business planning burdens, which additionally imposed late-stage interconnection fees will greatly

exacerbate. Requiring these highly mature projects to incur such expenses during a transitional

regulatory period misaligns the state’s economic development interests with already well-studied

load requests that, at build-out, will strengthen the reliability of the Texas electrical grid.

   II.     PROPOSED EVIDENCE SUPPORTING PROJECT MATURITY CRITERIA

         Project No. 58481 currently proposes certain site development maturity qualifiers,

including: (i) site control; (ii) site-related and engineering studies; and (iii) state and local permits

and approvals. While these qualifiers should not be treated as exhaustive for purposes of waiving

any $/MW requirements referenced above in Section I, additional clarity from the Commission

regarding the form and sufficiency of documentation needed to satisfy these requirements would

help provide greater certainty. An ILLE’s ability to provide verifiable evidence to ERCOT

demonstrating satisfaction of these maturity criteria may further support both (i) qualification for

treatment as proposed Batch Zero “base load” and (ii) corresponding waiver of any proposed

$/MW fee, particularly when considered in conjunction with demonstrated advancement in the

ERCOT interconnection process, including executed interconnection agreements, financial

commitments, and study progression.

    Accordingly, for purposes of demonstrating compliance with these maturity qualifiers, the

Commission should consider adopting the following documentation for submission to ERCOT:

    1. Site Control. One of the following:
            a. A recorded deed identifying the ILLE as the fee simple owner entity;
            b. A recorded ground lease, or memorandum thereof, identifying the ILLE as lessee
                for a term of five years or greater;
            c. Documentation demonstrating that an affiliated entity holds fee title or a qualifying
                leasehold interest in the site, together with an organizational chart and supporting
                documentation sufficient to verify the ILLE’s affiliation with such entity; or

                                                   4
             d. Other documentation demonstrating enforceable site control rights, including a
               purchase and sale agreement, option agreement, or similar instrument conferring
               the right to develop and operate the project at the site.
   2. Site-Related Studies and Engineering Services. Documentation demonstrating material
       advancement of site design and engineering, such as:
            a. Civil engineering plans; or
            b. Electrical design plans;
               in each case, together with at least one of the following:
            c. American Land Title Association (“ALTA”) survey or comparable study;
            d. Architectural or facility design plans;
            e. Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (“EPC”) plans;
            f. Engineering, Procurement, and Construction Management (“EPCM”) plans; or
            g. A geotechnical engineering report.
   3. State and Local Permits and Approvals. Documentation demonstrating material
       progress toward obtaining required governmental approvals for construction and operation
       of the project, such as:
            a. A zoning verification letter, or equivalent land use determination, confirming that
               the proposed use is permitted;
            b. Water and wastewater utility service availability confirmation, such as ‘will serve’
               letter(s) from the applicable water and wastewater provider(s), evidencing the
               availability of sufficient capacity to serve the project; or
            c. A recorded subdivision plat, or equivalent site development approval, for the
               project location.

       In addition, Skybox recommends that such submission(s) should be accompanied by an

attestation executed by an officer or other authorized representative of the submitting ILLE with

authority to bind the entity, certifying that the information provided is complete and accurate as of

the date of execution.

     III.    OFFSET OF FINANCIAL REQUIREMENTS BY EXISTING DEPOSITS

       For Batch Zero loads that do not qualify as “base load"—i.e., projects that have not yet

                                                  5
 satisfied Planning Guide §§ 9.4 and 9.5 through completion of required studies, execution of

interconnection agreements, and demonstration of financial commitment— the Commission

should ensure that any new financial requirements are calculated on a net basis, with full credit

given to amounts already posted with or paid to the applicable TDSP. Absent such a framework,

projects that have already demonstrated substantial financial commitment would be subject to

duplicative or overlapping collateral obligations for the same interconnection related scope.

       To avoid this outcome, the rule should expressly recognize and credit, on a first dollar basis,

all prior financial commitments that correspond to TDSP determined interconnection related costs,

including: (i) financial security posted for long lead equipment and necessary interconnection

services; and (ii) Contributions in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”) paid for transmission facilities,

substation upgrades, and other direct or ‘but-for’ system improvements. These amounts reflect

project specific cost causation and should be treated as satisfying, or at a minimum reducing, any

new financial obligations imposed under § 25.194.

       A netting approach is necessary to maintain alignment with PURA and Commission

precedent, which require that financial obligations be tied to actual system costs and risks rather

than imposed on a duplicative or standardized basis. Requiring additional deposits without

recognizing existing TDSP held amounts would result in “double collateralization,” creating

capital inefficiencies without providing incremental reliability or procurement assurance benefits.

This concern is particularly acute for projects that have already funded long lead equipment or

advanced construction activities in reliance on the existing interconnection framework.

Therefore, the Commission should clarify that any interconnection fee or similar financial

requirement must be reduced by the amount of existing deposits or payments held by the TDSP

that are attributable to the same interconnection related facilities, equipment, or services. This



                                                 6
 crediting should occur sequentially and consistently across all applicable financial provisions to

ensure that obligations are not duplicated across different components of the framework.

For example, for a 600 MW project subject to a $50,000/MW requirement (totaling $30 million),

where the ILLE has already provided $15 million in financial security and $5.5 million in CIAC

aligned with TDSP identified interconnection costs, the applicable obligation should be reduced

by the full $20.5 million already on deposit. In that case, only the incremental $9.5 million

difference should be required at the time of execution of a binding interconnection agreement.

         This approach is consistent with the Commission’s objectives under SB 6 and PURA §

37.0561 to support business development, minimize stranded infrastructure costs, and maintain

system reliability. It preserves appropriate protection for TDSPs and ratepayers by ensuring that

sufficient financial commitments are in place to cover interconnection related costs, while avoiding

duplicative requirements that would impose unnecessary and unforeseen capital burdens on

projects that have already made substantial, project specific investments.

   IV.      NON-CUMULATIVE TREATMENT OF FINANCIAL SECURITY ACROSS
                          DEVELOPMENT STAGES

         The Commission should clarify in 16 TAC § 25.194 that financial security requirements

associated with the intermediate agreement and the final interconnection agreement are not

cumulative, but instead represent a single, continuous financial commitment that evolves as the

project advances. Absent such clarification, the rule could be interpreted to require duplicative

postings that materially exceed the level of commitment necessary to demonstrate project viability

and manage interconnection risk.


         Accordingly, Skybox recommends a single total financial commitment of $50,000/MW,

structured to reflect the progression of project maturity. At the intermediate stage, the $50,000/MW

amount would be required but remain largely refundable (e.g., 85%), preserving flexibility during

                                                 7
 early development while still demonstrating meaningful commitment. Upon execution of the final

interconnection agreement, that same $50,000/MW amount would remain on deposit but transition

to a non-refundable structure, reflecting the project’s advancement and increased certainty.


          This approach ensures that ILLEs maintain appropriate “skin in the game” throughout the

development lifecycle and aligns financial requirements with actual project risk, supports

continued investment in large scale infrastructure, and advances the Commission’s objectives

under SB 6 to promote business development while maintaining system reliability and minimizing

unnecessary cost burdens.


     V.       ADJUSTED REFUNDABILITY FOR ALLOCATION SHORTAGES AND
                                  DELAYS

          The Commission should ensure that any $/MW based financial requirement under 16 TAC

§ 25.194 is grounded in the practical realities of system deliverability and TDSP controlled

interconnection outcomes. In particular, refundability provisions associated with financial

commitments under the final interconnection agreement should be calibrated to account for

circumstances in which the level or timing of service ultimately provided materially deviates from

the capacity and schedule requested and relied upon by the ILLE.


          Accordingly, Skybox recommends that refundability conditions be adjusted in two discrete

scenarios: (i) where a project is allocated less capacity than originally requested (“Under

Allocation”); and (ii) where the delivery of service is materially delayed beyond the requested

interconnection load ramp date (“Significant Delay”).


A.        Under Allocation (Pro Rata Adjustment Mechanism)

          Where the MW capacity ultimately made available by the TDSP is less than the amount


                                                 8
 requested and reflected in the interconnection agreement, the applicable financial obligation

should be reduced on a proportional (per MW) basis. Any financial security, interconnection fee,

or other deposit attributable to undelivered capacity should be refunded or credited to the

interconnecting customer.

     Mechanically, this can be implemented by applying a simple pro rata adjustment:
        Adjusted Obligation = (Delivered MW ÷ Requested MW) × Total Required Financial
         Commitment

        Refund/Credit = Total Amount on Deposit – Adjusted Obligation

     This approach ensures that financial commitments remain directly tied to the level of service

actually provided and avoids requiring ILLEs to bear costs for capacity that is not delivered,

consistent with cost causation principles.

B.       Significant Delay (Time-Based Refundability Adjustment)

         Where service delivery is materially delayed beyond the requested interconnection load

ramp date, refundability provisions should be adjusted to reflect the diminished value of delayed

service and the increased development risk borne by the project. For purposes of administrability,

a “Significant Delay” could be defined as a delay exceeding three (3) years from the requested

load ramp date specified in the interconnection agreement or associated study assumptions.

In such cases, the rule should provide that:

        A defined portion of the financial commitment (e.g., a specified percentage of the $/MW
         amount) reverts to refundable status; or

        The customer is entitled to a full refund or credit with formal withdrawal of its request, less
         actual costs incurred by TSP for engineering studies and procurement efforts that cannot
         be repurposed;

provided that the delay is not attributable to the interconnecting customer and is instead driven by

system constraints, study sequencing, or other factors outside of the customer’s control.



                                                   9
 C.       Implementation and Interaction with Existing Financial Framework

     These refundability adjustments should operate in conjunction with the crediting framework

described in Section II and the non-cumulative structure described in Section III. Specifically:

        Refund and credit calculations should be applied after giving effect to first-dollar crediting
         of existing financial security and CIAC;

        No portion of the required financial commitment should be subject to forfeiture for
         undelivered capacity or delay driven deferrals outside the customer’s control; and

        TDSPs should retain the ability to require incremental financial commitments only to the
         extent necessary to cover actual interconnection related costs associated with delivered
         capacity.

     These refinements are consistent with SB 6 and PURA § 37.0561, which require that

interconnection standards support business development while maintaining system reliability and

minimizing stranded infrastructure costs. By tying financial obligations to actual deliverability and

timing—rather than static assumptions—the Commission can preserve appropriate system

protections while avoiding outcomes that would impose disproportionate or unintended financial

burdens on projects that have already made substantial investments in reliance on the

interconnection framework.

             VI.     NON-UTILIZED CAPACITY TIMING CONSIDERATIONS

         Project No. 58481 currently proposes that, not later than 30 days after an ILLE fails by six

(6) months to satisfy a milestone in its phased energization schedule, the interconnecting TDSP

must notify ERCOT of the ILLE’s non-utilized capacity. Within 60 days, the TDSP must initiate

draw-down on unused financial security posted by the ILLE for costs incurred by the TDSP in

fulfilling the large load interconnection request, including: (i) equipment that has been procured

and cannot be canceled for a full refund; (ii) construction that has commenced and cannot be

canceled for a full refund; and (iii) services that have been initiated and cannot be canceled for a


                                                  10
 full refund.

        Given the magnitude of concurrent changes associated with implementation of revised

large load interconnection processes and oversight frameworks, the Commission should consider

deferring rulemaking on non-utilized capacity to a subsequent proceeding, after sufficient

operational experience has been gained under the proposed batch framework and a more stable

implementation cadence has been established.

        Alternatively, if the Commission elects to address non-utilized capacity in this proceeding,

Skybox recommends that the rule include an initial three-year buffer from the commencement of

phased energization. In addition, the rule should provide a six-month cure period for the ILLE to

remedy any milestone deficiency, including by demonstrating progress toward the applicable

milestone, revising the phased energization schedule with supporting justification, or otherwise

curing the deficiency. This approach supports continued advancement of large load interconnection

projects during an initial implementation, while providing time for the revised framework to be

applied in practice and for associated processes and timelines to stabilize.

                                      VII.    CONCLUSION

        In sum, the Commission’s implementation of 16 TAC § 25.194 presents a significant

opportunity to establish a durable, coherent framework for large load interconnection that advances

the objectives of SB 6 and PURA § 37.0561. As demonstrated above, stakeholders have invested

substantial time, resources, and capital in reliance on the existing large load interconnection

framework and in active participation in ERCOT’s stakeholder processes addressing Batch Zero

eligibility and broader large load integration.

        To ensure that the resulting framework supports continued investment while maintaining

system reliability, it is essential that the Commission adopt standards that are prospective,


                                                  11
 grounded in cost-causation principles, and calibrated to actual system risk and deliverability. This

includes recognizing the status of advanced-stage projects, avoiding duplicative or cumulative

financial requirements, crediting existing financial commitments, and ensuring that refundability

provisions appropriately reflect real-world interconnection outcomes.

       Clear and definitive direction in this rulemaking will provide the regulatory certainty

necessary for project sponsors and capital providers to continue advancing large-scale

infrastructure in Texas, while also enabling ERCOT and TDSPs to implement a consistent,

administrable, and reliability-focused interconnection framework. By aligning financial

requirements with actual system conditions and preserving reliance on prior compliance, the

Commission can achieve its statutory objectives without imposing unnecessary or unintended

barriers to development.



Date: April 10, 2026                                 Respectfully submitted,




                                                     Haynes Strader
                                                     Chief Development Officer
                                                     Skybox Datacenters, LLC

                                        EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
   Advanced-Stage (Base Load / Batch Zero) Project Treatment
       o Recognize projects meeting Planning Guide §§ 9.4/9.5 as advanced-stage

       o ILLE Attestation
   Netting of Financial Requirements (No Double Collateralization)
        o Require first-dollar crediting of existing TDSP-held amounts (security, CIAC)

   Non-Cumulative Financial Security Structure
       o Clarify intermediate and final security are not cumulative
       o Establish single total obligation ($50,000/MW)
              Intermediate Agreement: refundable (e.g., ~85%)
              Interconnection Agreement: same amount becomes non-refundable
       o Avoid duplicative ($100,000/MW) burden; align with project maturity and risk progression
   Refundability Adjustments (Deliverability-Based)
       o Under-Allocation
                Pro rata where delivered MW < requested MW
                Refund/credit for undelivered capacity
                Adjusted = (Delivered ÷ Requested) × Total; Refund = Deposit – Adjusted
       o Significant Delay
                Define delay (e.g., > 3 years from requested ramp; not caused by ILLE)
                Full refund or reversion to refundable status, less actuated costs
       o Implementation
                Apply after security/CIAC crediting; no forfeiture for undelivered capacity or system delays
                Limit TDSP recovery to delivered-capacity costs
   Non-Utilized Capacity Timing Considerations
       o Defer rulemaking pending implementation experience with revised framework
       o If addressed in 58481: Establish initial 3-year buffer from phased energization; provide 6-month cure
           period for milestone deficiencies

all prior financial commitments that correspond to TDSP determined interconnection related costs,

including: (i) financial security posted for long lead equipment and necessary interconnection

services; and (ii) Contributions in Aid of Construction ("CIAC") paid for transmission facilities,

substation upgrades, and other direct or 'but-for' system improvements. These amounts reflect

project specific cost causation and should be treated as satisfying, or at a minimum reducing, any

new financial obligations imposed under § 25.194.

       A netting approach is necessary to maintain alignment with PURA and Commission

precedent, which require that financial obligations be tied to actual system costs and risks rather

than imposed on a duplicative or standardized basis. Requiring additional deposits without

recognizing existing TDSP held amounts would result in "double collateralization," creating

capital inefficiencies without providing incremental reliability or procurement assurance benefits.

This concern is particularly acute for projects that have already funded long lead equipment or

advanced construction activities in reliance on the existing interconnection framework.

Therefore, the Commission should clarify that any interconnection fee or similar financial

requirement must be reduced by the amount of existing deposits or payments held by the TDSP

that are attributable to the same interconnection related facilities, equipment, or services. This



                                                  6
 crediting should occur sequentially and consistently across all applicable financial provisions to

ensure that obligations are not duplicated across different components ofthe framework.

For example, for a 600 MW project subject to a $50,000/MW requirement (totaling $30 million),

where the ILLE has already provided $15 million in financial security and $5.5 million in CIAC

aligned with TDSP identified interconnection costs, the applicable obligation should be reduced

by the full $20.5 million already on deposit. In that case, only the incremental $9.5 million

difference should be required at the time of execution of a binding interconnection agreement.

         This approach is consistent with the Commission's objectives under SB 6 and PURA §

37.0561 to support business development, minimize stranded infrastructure costs, and maintain

system reliability. It preserves appropriate protection for TDSPs and ratepayers by ensuring that

sufficient financial commitments are in place to cover interconnection related costs, while avoiding

duplicative requirements that would impose unnecessary and unforeseen capital burdens on

projects that have already made substantial, project specific investments.

   IV.      NON-CUMULATIVE TREATMENT OF FINANCIAL SECURITY ACROSS
                                   DEVELOPMENTSTAGES
         The Commission should clarify in 16 TAC § 25.194 that financial security requirements

associated with the intermediate agreement and the final interconnection agreement are not

cumulative, but instead represent a single, continuous financial commitment that evolves as the

project advances. Absent such clarification, the rule could be interpreted to require duplicative

postings that materially exceed the level of commitment necessary to demonstrate proj ect viability

and manage interconnection risk.


         Accordingly, Skybox recommends a single total financial commitment of $50,000/MW,

structured to reflect the progression of project maturity. Atthe intermediate stage, the $50,000/MW

amount would be required but remain largely refundable (e.g., 85%), preserving flexibility during

                                                 7
 early development while still demonstrating meaningful commitment. Upon execution of the final

interconnection agreement, that same $50,000/MW amount would remain on deposit but transition

to a non-refundable structure, reflecting the project's advancement and increased certainty.


          This approach ensures that ILLEs maintain appropriate "skin in the game" throughout the

development lifecycle and aligns financial requirements with actual proj ect risk, supports

continued investment in large scale infrastructure, and advances the Commission's objectives

under SB 6 to promote business development while maintaining system reliability and minimizing

unnecessary cost burdens.


     V.       ADJUSTED REFUNDABILITY FOR ALLOCATION SHORTAGES AND
                                             DELAYS
          The Commission should ensure that any $/MW based financial requirement under 16 TAC

§ 25.194 is grounded in the practical realities of system deliverability and TDSP controlled

interconnection outcomes. In particular, refundability provisions associated with financial

commitments under the final interconnection agreement should be calibrated to account for

circumstances in which the level or timing of service ultimately provided materially deviates from

the capacity and schedule requested and relied upon by the ILLE.


          Accordingly, Skybox recommends that refundability conditions be adjusted in two discrete

scenarios: (i) where a project is allocated less capacity than originally requested ("Under

Allocation"); and (ii) where the delivery of service is materially delayed beyond the requested

interconnection load ramp date ("Significant Delay").


A.        Under Allocation (Pro Rata Adjustment Mechanism)

          Where the MW capacity ultimately made available by the TDSP is less than the amount


                                                 8
 requested and reflected in the interconnection agreement, the applicable financial obligation

should be reduced on a proportional (per MW) basis. Any financial security, interconnection fee,

or other deposit attributable to undelivered capacity should be refunded or credited to the

interconnecting customer.

     Mechanically, this can be implemented by applying a simple pro ram adjustment:
     •   Adjusted Obligation == (Delivered MW + Requested MW) x Total Required Financial
         Commitment

     •   Refund/Credit = Total Amount on Deposit - Adjusted Obligation

     This approach ensures that financial commitments remain directly tied to the level of service

actually provided and avoids requiring ILLEs to bear costs for capacity that is not delivered,

consistent with cost causation principles.

B.       Significant Delay (Time-Based Refundability Adjustment)

         Where service delivery is materially delayed beyond the requested interconnection load

ramp date, refundability provisions should be adjusted to reflect the diminished value of delayed

service and the increased development risk borne by the proj ect. For purposes of administrability,

a "Significant Delay" could be defined as a delay exceeding three (3) years from the requested

load ramp date specified in the interconnection agreement or associated study assumptions.

In such cases, the rule should provide that:

     •   A defined portion of the financial commitment (e.g., a specified percentage of the $/MW
         amount) reverts to refundable status; or

     •   The customer is entitled to a full refund or credit with formal withdrawal of its request, less
         actual costs incurred by TSP for engineering studies and procurement efforts that cannot
         be repurposed;

provided that the delay is not attributable to the interconnecting customer and is instead driven by

system constraints, study sequencing, or other factors outside of the customer's control.



                                                    9
 C.       Implementation and Interaction with Existing Financial Framework

     These refundability adjustments should operate in conjunction with the crediting framework

described in Section II and the non-cumulative structure described in Section III. Specifically:

     •   Refund and credit calculations should be applied after giving effect to first-dollar crediting
         of existing financial security and CIAC;

     •   No portion of the required financial commitment should be subject to forfeiture for
         undelivered capacity or delay driven deferrals outside the customer's control; and

     •   TDSPs should retain the ability to require incremental financial commitments only to the
         extent necessary to cover actual interconnection related costs associated with delivered
         capacity.

     These refinements are consistent with SB 6 and PURA § 37.0561, which require that

interconnection standards support business development while maintaining system reliability and

minimizing stranded infrastructure costs. By tying financial obligations to actual deliverability and

timing-rather than static assumptions-the Commission can preserve appropriate system

protections while avoiding outcomes that would impose disproportionate or unintended financial

burdens on projects that have already made substantial investments in reliance on the

interconnection framework.

             VI.     NON-UTILIZED CAPACITY TIMING CONSIDERATIONS

         Project No. 58481 currently proposes that, not later than 30 days after an ILLE fails by six

(6) months to satisfy a milestone in its phased energization schedule, the interconnecting TDSP

must notify ERCOT of the ILLE's non-utilized capacity. Within 60 days, the TDSP must initiate

draw-down on unused financial security posted by the ILLE for costs incurred by the TDSP in

fulfilling the large load interconnection request, including: (i) equipment that has been procured

and cannot be canceled for a full refund; (ii) construction that has commenced and cannot be

canceled for a full refund; and (iii) services that have been initiated and cannot be canceled for a


                                                    10
 full refund.

        Given the magnitude of concurrent changes associated with implementation of revised

large load interconnection processes and oversight frameworks, the Commission should consider

deferring rulemaking on non-utilized capacity to a subsequent proceeding, after sufficient

operational experience has been gained under the proposed batch framework and a more stable

implementation cadence has been established.

        Alternatively, ifthe Commission elects to address non-utilized capacity in this proceeding,

Skybox recommends that the rule include an initial three-year buffer from the commencement of

phased energization. In addition, the rule should provide a six-month cure period for the ILLE to

remedy any milestone deficiency, including by demonstrating progress toward the applicable

milestone, revising the phased energization schedule with supporting justification, or otherwise

curing the deficiency. This approach supports continued advancement oflarge load interconnection

projects during an initial implementation, while providing time for the revised framework to be

applied in practice and for associated processes and timelines to stabilize.

                                      VII.    CONCLUSION

        In sum, the Commission's implementation of 16 TAC § 25.194 presents a significant

opportunity to establish a durable, coherent framework for large load interconnection that advances

the objectives of SB 6 and PURA § 37.0561. As demonstrated above, stakeholders have invested

substantial time, resources, and capital in reliance on the existing large load interconnection

framework and in active participation in ERCOT's stakeholder processes addressing Batch Zero

eligibility and broader large load integration.

        To ensure that the resulting framework supports continued investment while maintaining

system reliability, it is essential that the Commission adopt standards that are prospective,


                                                  11
 grounded in cost-causation principles, and calibrated to actual system risk and deliverability. This

includes recognizing the status of advanced-stage proj ects, avoiding duplicative or cumulative

financial requirements, crediting existing financial commitments, and ensuring that refundability

provisions appropriately reflect real-world interconnection outcomes.

       Clear and definitive direction in this rulemaking will provide the regulatory certainty

necessary for project sponsors and capital providers to continue advancing large-scale

infrastructure in Texas, while also enabling ERCOT and TDSPs to implement a consistent,

administrable,   and reliability-focused interconnection framework.        By aligning financial

requirements with actual system conditions and preserving reliance on prior compliance, the

Commission can achieve its statutory obj ectives without imposing unnecessary or unintended

barriers to development.
